extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners before the USPTO (patent/trademark lawyers), and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for assessing practitioner conduct, jurisdiction, procedural compliance, and sanctions in USPTO disciplinary proceedings and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Disciplinary Jurisdiction over Practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may assert disciplinary jurisdiction over attorneys who practice before the Office (including trademark practitioners) in trademark or patent matters; lack of knowledge or ignorance of the USPTO's rules is not relevant to the finding of jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings and resources (e.g., TMEP § 601, the Code of Federal Regulations, and OED's website) are readily available; presence of links in filing documents and on the Agency website provide notice. Prior decisions (e.g., In re Blackowicz) support assertion of jurisdiction over practitioners who practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized Practice of Patent Law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's regulations; the USPTO is a 'jurisdiction' for purposes of § 11.505. Only practitioners registered under § 11.6 are permitted to prosecute patent applications of others before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities constituting practice before the Office include reviewing/drafting responses to Notices/Office Actions, making arguments about patentability, drafting/revising patent applications (specifications, claims, drawings), advising on patent strategy, preparing CIPs and PCT filings. Prior USPTO precedents (Wengrovsky, Gaudio) show trademark practitioners providing such services can be disciplined for unauthorized patent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Decline or Withdraw When Representation Would Violate Rules (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must decline representation of a client, or withdraw, where representation will violate USPTO Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the practitioner's intended services would constitute unauthorized practice (see § 11.505), the practitioner is required to decline or withdraw; providing services despite this duty supports a violation of § 11.116.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or Misleading Communications (37 C.F.R. § 11.701)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications about the practitioner or the practitioner's services are false or misleading if they contain a material misrepresentation of fact or law or omit a fact necessary to prevent the statement from being materially misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 11.701 does not require proof of intent or knowledge; ignorance of the law or reliance on third-party commentary (e.g., a blog) is not a defense. Example in record: statements to a client that non-registered attorney assistance while the client proceeds pro se was permissible were found false and misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Prejudicial to the Administration of Justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) & § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibited conduct includes behavior that 'impedes or subverts the process of resolving disputes' or 'frustrates the fair balance of interests or "justice" essential to litigation or other proceedings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attorney's behavior that negatively impacts the public's perception of the legal system or undermines confidence in the system can be prejudicial; the unauthorized practice of law has been found to threaten the effective administration of justice and thus satisfy this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Prior USPTO and Court Precedent in Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior disciplinary proceedings and court decisions (e.g., Wengrovsky, Gaudio, Blackowicz) are used to determine whether similar conduct amounts to unauthorized practice and to assess appropriate discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in procedural posture do not necessarily remove the precedential value for jurisdictional or substantive determinations; distinctions about the severity of misconduct are relevant to sanction determination, not necessarily to the threshold question of unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for Imposing Exclusion or Suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: An ALJ must explain the reason for imposing exclusion or suspension after considering four factors: (1) whether a duty was violated to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether conduct was intentional/knowing/negligent; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ's sanction explanation must address these factors on the record; the significance/degree of misconduct bears primarily on sanction, not on whether a violation occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof for Affirmative Defenses (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have the burden of proving any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to produce clear and convincing evidence supporting affirmative defenses (waiver, laches, unclean hands, estoppel, constitutional claims, statutory overreach, etc.) will result in rejection of those defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate Brief Filing Requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.55; incorporation of FRAP rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate briefs must comply with substantive and form requirements found in FRAP (Rule 28 and Rule 32) as incorporated by § 11.55; an appellant/appellee brief shall be no more than thirty pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In computing length limits FRAP 32(f) provides that cover page, table of contents, and table of citations do not count toward the page limit; adopting that practice is persuasive and consistent with prior disciplinary appeals. The USPTO Director may refuse entry of a nonconforming brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena Procedure and Admission of Subpoenaed Evidence (35 U.S.C. § 24; 37 C.F.R. § 11.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 24, the clerk of a U.S. district court shall issue a subpoena for witnesses on application; evidence obtained by a subpoena issued under 35 U.S.C. § 24 shall not be admitted into the record or considered unless leave to proceed under § 24 was previously authorized by the hearing officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for subpoenas must be timely; the hearing officer has discretion to deny late subpoena requests (e.g., less than two business days before hearing). Remote testimony arrangements may require advance equipment reservations; lack of diligence in securing voluntary attendance or timely subpoenas undercuts claims of prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due Process Requirements in Disciplinary Proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Due process requires reasonable notice of charges and a meaningful opportunity to be heard, including presenting evidence, testifying, cross-examining witnesses, and presenting argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation in hearings with opportunity to present and challenge evidence generally satisfies due process; claims that constitutional due process was violated must be adequately pleaded and developed, and unsupported or undeveloped constitutional assertions may be deemed waived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Evidence of 'Practice Before the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.5 defines 'practice before the Office' and identifies activities that constitute practice in patent matters (see § 11.5 and § 11.5(b)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record may include testimony, invoices, documents showing performance of tasks such as drafting patent applications, responding to Office actions, preparing claims, and advising on prosecution strategy; such evidence supports findings of practice before the Office even if the practitioner did not sign filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of Rules or Reliance on Third-Party Commentary Is Not a Defense
rubrics_metrics.description: General principle that 'ignorance of a statute is generally no defense' applies: lack of knowledge of USPTO rules or reliance on third-party authorities (e.g., blogs) does not excuse violations of disciplinary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority includes Torres v. INS; § 11.701 and related rules do not require intent. Reliance on purportedly authoritative commentators is irrelevant to establishing absence of violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and Diligence in Securing Witness Testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A party seeking witness testimony (voluntary or via subpoena) must be diligent and timely in attempting to secure that testimony; late attempts may be denied and may not constitute prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hearing location and date were known well in advance, waiting until less than two business days before the hearing to seek remote subpoena or to arrange testimony undermines a claim that denial of subpoena prejudiced the party. Hearing officers may allow voluntary appearances but are not required to compel belatedly requested testimony.
